title: Keep Easter fifty days
tomorrow: a sound like wind, and each visitor hears their own language. how?

cards: Lent gets the plans. The sweets go, the prayers come, the days are counted. Then Easter Sunday arrives, the flowers come out, the big meal is eaten, and by Monday the house is back to normal.
So why would anyone keep celebrating for weeks? Because in the church calendar, Easter isn't one day. It's a season, and it's meant to last.

teach.b: In the church year of churches that keep it, Easter runs fifty days, from the empty tomb to Pentecost. The Bible gives that stretch its feel.
Acts says the risen Jesus showed himself to his friends over forty days, speaking of the kingdom of God.

And Luke ends his Gospel with them after he is taken up, in the King James Bible: “And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy.” Joy is where Luke leaves them. Here's the hard part.
Fasting has rules, so it feels like discipline. Celebrating sounds easy, but it slips away by Tuesday.
Paul writes: “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.” He says it twice, as an instruction, not a mood. Joy here is something practiced, the way a fast is.
So the fifty days ask for the same care Lent did: a plan.
A meal with friends, music turned up, flowers on the table, a walk somewhere beautiful, thanks said on purpose.

how: In the church calendar of churches that keep the Christian year, Easter is a season that runs from Easter Sunday to Pentecost; some Christians mark it with feasting, flowers, music and Easter greetings.

games.q: what does “keep easter fifty days” mean?
o: celebrating Easter as a season, not a single day
a fifty-day countdown leading up to Easter
fasting for fifty days after Easter Sunday

games.q: the last six lines — tap the pairs.

s: Luke's Gospel ends with the disciples hiding in fear
it ends with them returning to Jerusalem with great joy.
in the church year, Easter is a season, not a single day
it runs fifty days, from Easter Sunday to Pentecost.
Paul says rejoice only once, as a passing thought
he says it twice: rejoice, and again I say, rejoice.

games.q: your friend says Easter Monday always feels like a letdown after all of Lent's effort. what does the church year offer her?
o: keep celebrating: Easter is a season, fifty days long.
start planning next year's Lent right away instead.
accept it: joy always fades by Monday morning.
games.why: Easter runs fifty days to Pentecost, and Paul says rejoice twice, as an instruction. joy can be planned as carefully as a fast.

practice: Put on one piece of music that sounds like joy to you, or listen for a glad sound nearby: a laugh, a bird, a kettle starting to sing. Let it play through the sit.
While it does, choose one joy to plan for a coming week, a meal, a walk, flowers on a table, and give it a day.

wordCard.voice: Keep Easter fifty days. A season of joy as long as the fast before it, kept with as much care.

orig.note: the Greek word for joy, as in Luke's 'great joy'.

carryVoice: Your line: fifty days of joy. Fourteen lines in two weeks, and this one gets celebrated. Two weeks, done.
